quiz_met3:1.q: A rapidly dividing cell oxidizes glucose through the pentose phosphate pathway instead of glycolysis. Which end product does this route yield?
quiz_met3:1.r: Glucose has three fates: storage as glycogen, oxidation via the pentose phosphate pathway to ribose 5-phosphate, and oxidation via glycolysis to pyruvate (p. 649).

quiz_met3:10.q: After a sugary meal, a hepatocyte keeps phosphorylating glucose even though glucose 6-phosphate (G6P) has built up. Which enzyme property explains this?
o: Hexokinase I is activated by G6P
Hexokinase II is not inhibited by G6P
Glucokinase is inhibited by high ATP
Glucokinase is not inhibited by G6P
quiz_met3:10.r: Liver glucokinase (hexokinase IV) responds only to higher glucose (10 mM) and is not inhibited by G6P, so it keeps trapping excess glucose in the liver after a meal; hexokinases I to III are inhibited by G6P (p. 657).

quiz_met3:11.q: A researcher wants to block the first reaction that commits glucose to glycolysis while leaving glycogen synthesis from glucose 6-phosphate intact. Which enzyme should be inhibited?
quiz_met3:11.r: Phosphofructokinase-1 (step 3) is the irreversible step that commits glucose to glycolysis (p. 658); hexokinase is irreversible but does not commit (p. 656).

quiz_met3:12.q: A resting myocyte with a full energy charge slows glycolysis at phosphofructokinase-1. Which allosteric signal inhibits this enzyme?
quiz_met3:12.r: Phosphofructokinase-1 is allosterically inhibited by high ATP and stimulated by high ADP and AMP (p. 658).

quiz_met3:13.q: A 17-year-old has exercise-induced calf pain, elevated creatine kinase, mild hemolysis, and pools of glycogen-like material on muscle biopsy. Which enzyme is most likely defective?
quiz_met3:13.r: Defective muscle phosphofructokinase (PFKM) is glycogen storage disease type VII, Tarui disease: severe muscle glycolysis defect plus glycogenosis associated with hemolysis (p. 659, p. 680; case on p. 646).

quiz_met3:14.q: A patient with Tarui disease has severe muscle symptoms but only mild hemolysis. Why is glycolysis in his red cells only about 50% impaired?
o: They express only the L isoform
They express only the P isoform
They express both M and L isoforms
They express M and P isoforms only
They bypass the PFK step entirely
quiz_met3:14.r: Red blood cells express both PFKM and PFKL, so defective PFKM gives a severe defect in muscle glycolysis but only a 50% defect in red cell glycolysis (p. 659).

quiz_met3:15.q: In a cell, the kinase form of PFK2 raises fructose 2,6-bisphosphate. What is the effect on PFK-1 and on fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase (FBPase)?
quiz_met3:15.r: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6-BP on the slide) activates PFK-1 and inhibits fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, pushing flux toward glycolysis (p. 660).

quiz_met3:16.q: In step 6 of glycolysis, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate is oxidized and phosphorylated to 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate. What supplies the phosphate group added in this step?
quiz_met3:16.r: At glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase the phosphate comes from inorganic phosphate (Pi), not ATP; the step also reduces one NAD+ per triose (p. 661).

quiz_met3:17.q: An inhibitor added to a red cell lysate blocks the first substrate-level phosphorylation of glycolysis. Which intermediate, the substrate of the blocked enzyme, accumulates?
quiz_met3:17.r: Phosphoglycerate kinase (step 7) is the first substrate-level phosphorylation: 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate phosphorylates ADP, giving 3-phosphoglycerate and ATP (p. 662, p. 655).

quiz_met3:18.q: A mutation abolishes the enzyme that catalyzes the irreversible ATP-forming step of glycolysis. Which substrate can no longer be converted to its product?
quiz_met3:18.r: Pyruvate kinase (step 10) is irreversible and is the second substrate-level phosphorylation, using phosphoenolpyruvate (p. 663); phosphoglycerate kinase also makes ATP but is reversible (p. 662), and PFK-1 is irreversible but uses ATP (p. 658).

quiz_met3:19.q: A student proposes that human liver could turn acetyl-CoA back into pyruvate by running the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction backward. Why is this impossible?
o: It is irreversible with no bypass
It requires oxygen as a substrate
It is absent from liver cells
It commits carbon to the cycle
quiz_met3:19.r: Pyruvate dehydrogenase is an irreversible reaction with no bypass in vertebrates; it does NOT commit carbon to the citric acid cycle, and it requires thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2) and niacin (B3) (p. 666).

quiz_met3:2.q: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, a hepatocyte holds more glucose than it needs for energy. Into which products does the liver convert this excess glucose?
quiz_met3:2.r: In liver, excess glucose is converted to fatty acids or to glycogen; the liver's primary job is to maintain blood glucose (p. 651).

quiz_met3:20.q: A man with chronic alcohol use disorder develops confusion, ataxia and ocular abnormalities. The vitamin he lacks is required by which of these enzymes?
quiz_met3:20.r: Confusion, ataxia and ocular abnormalities are Wernicke's encephalopathy, a thiamine (B1) deficiency (p. 667); pyruvate dehydrogenase requires vitamin B1 (p. 666).

quiz_met3:21.q: A patient with auto-brewery syndrome has a raised blood alcohol level without drinking. His gut microbes ferment pyruvate using which enzyme that mammals lack?
quiz_met3:21.r: Pyruvate decarboxylase (pyruvate to acetaldehyde + CO2) is not present in mammals but is present in the gut microbiome; alcohol dehydrogenase is present in mammals (p. 672, p. 673).

quiz_met3:22.q: A child has a congenital deficiency of sucrase-isomaltase. According to the lecture, hydrolysis of which two disaccharides is lost?
quiz_met3:22.r: Her hydrolysis slide writes sucrase-isomaltase under both maltose (to 2 glucose) and sucrose (to fructose + glucose); lactose is split by lactase (p. 675).

quiz_met3:23.q: A lactase-deficient adult drinks a glass of milk and develops bloating. What happens to the undigested lactose?
o: Yields acids and gas in large intestine
Is absorbed intact in the small intestine
Is converted to galactose in the liver
quiz_met3:23.r: Only monosaccharides can be absorbed (p. 675); without lactase, lactose passes to the large intestine, where acids and gas are produced (p. 676).

quiz_met3:24.q: An infant digests lactose and absorbs the galactose. As which intermediate do the galactose carbons join the glucose pathway, just before conversion to glucose 6-phosphate?
quiz_met3:24.r: Galactose passes through UDP-galactose and UDP-glucose to glucose 1-phosphate, which phosphoglucomutase converts to glucose 6-phosphate (p. 677, p. 678).

quiz_met3:25.q: A man drinks several liters of fructose-sweetened soda every day. According to the lecture, what is the predominant fate of the excess fructose in his liver?
quiz_met3:25.r: The fructose slide marks glycerol 3-phosphate plus acyl-CoA to acyl glycerols, then VLDL, as the predominant pathway after excessive fructose intake in liver (p. 679).

quiz_met3:3.q: A well-oxygenated neuron catabolizes glucose completely through glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. What are the end products of this aerobic catabolism?
quiz_met3:3.r: Aerobic glucose catabolism ends in CO2 and H2O: brain catabolizes glucose aerobically to CO2 and H2O (p. 651), and the map ends at 4 CO2 + 4 H2O after the citric acid cycle (p. 650).

quiz_met3:4.q: During an all-out sprint, a runner's quadriceps converts most of its pyruvate to lactate. What does this conversion provide that lets glycolysis continue?
quiz_met3:4.r: Muscle converts pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD+ when O2 is scarce, as in intense exercise (p. 651); glycolysis needs NAD+ as a cofactor to keep running (p. 665).

quiz_met3:5.q: Mature red blood cells circulate in oxygen-rich arterial blood yet convert their pyruvate to lactate. Which feature of these cells explains this?
quiz_met3:5.r: Red blood cells carry out anaerobic catabolism, converting pyruvate to lactate, because they lack mitochondria, the location of oxidative phosphorylation (p. 651).

quiz_met3:6.q: A muscle cell converts 5 molecules of glucose to pyruvate by glycolysis. What is the net yield of ATP and NADH?
quiz_met3:6.r: Net glycolysis gives 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose (p. 653, p. 680), so 5 glucose give 10 ATP and 10 NADH; 4 ATP per glucose is the gross payoff before subtracting the 2 ATP invested (p. 654, p. 655).

quiz_met3:7.q: A cell extract can carry out only the preparatory phase of glycolysis. Starting from one glucose, what is the result of this phase?
quiz_met3:7.r: The preparatory phase (steps 1 to 5) invests 2 ATP, at hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1, and generates 2 trioses; ATP and NADH are made only in the payoff phase (p. 654, p. 655).

quiz_met3:8.q: In a myocyte, hexokinase converts incoming glucose to glucose 6-phosphate. What does this irreversible step accomplish for the cell?
quiz_met3:8.r: The hexokinase step is irreversible and retains glucose in the cell, but it does not commit glucose to glycolysis, because glucose 6-phosphate can still go to glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway (p. 656).

quiz_met3:9.q: A fasting patient's blood glucose is 4.5 mM. Why do hexokinases I to III in his peripheral tissues stay active at this concentration?
o: They respond only above 10 mM glucose
They respond well to 0.1 mM glucose
They are expressed only in the liver
They are stimulated by ADP and AMP
quiz_met3:9.r: Hexokinases I, II and III respond well to low glucose (0.1 mM), so at a blood glucose of about 4 to 5 mM they always have enough glucose to be active; they are inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate (p. 657).

quiz_met3_b:1.q: Oxidation of glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate in step 6 of glycolysis has an unfavorable standard free energy change, yet it runs forward in a working myocyte. According to the lecture, what drives it forward?
quiz_met3_b:1.r: Phosphoglycerate kinase (step 7) 'consumes product of previous reaction, so necessary for driving that reaction in the forward direction' (p. 662); step 6 has a positive standard free energy change (p. 661). Tautomerization belongs to pyruvate kinase (p. 663).

quiz_met3_b:2.q: In a hepatocyte, PKA phosphorylates PFK2. According to the lecture's scheme, which form of PFK2 results, and what happens to fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP)?
quiz_met3_b:2.r: PKA adds a phosphate to PFK2, giving the phosphatase form, which breaks F2,6BP down to fructose 6-phosphate and Pi; the unphosphorylated kinase form makes F2,6BP, the activator of PFK-1 (p. 660).

quiz_met3_b:3.q: After an all-out sprint, a runner's leg muscles have made a large load of lactate. According to the lecture's lactate shuttle model, where does the largest share go?
quiz_met3_b:3.r: About 50% is transported to other tissues for energy production, about 25% stays in the muscle cell for oxidation in mitochondria and peroxisomes, and about 25% goes to the liver for gluconeogenesis (Cori cycle) (p. 671).

quiz_met3_b:4.q: A woman taking isoniazid develops a thick scaly rash on her face, neck and hands, with diarrhea and dementia. Which requirement of the pyruvate dehydrogenase reaction is she lacking?
quiz_met3_b:4.r: Pellagra is niacin (B3) deficiency: dermatitis in sun-exposed areas, diarrhea, dementia and death, with isoniazid listed as a secondary cause (p. 668). Pyruvate dehydrogenase requires B1, B2 and B3 (p. 666).

quiz_met3_b:5.q: A milk-fed newborn with hepatomegaly and hypoglycemia lacks the transferase that makes UDP-galactose. Which intermediate builds up directly behind the block?
quiz_met3_b:5.r: Galactokinase makes galactose 1-phosphate, and galactose 1-phosphate uridylyltransferase then converts it (with UDP-glucose) to UDP-galactose and glucose 1-phosphate; a defect in this enzyme is one cause of galactosemia (p. 678).

quiz_met3_b:6.q: A 6-month-old who thrived on breast milk becomes lethargic with severe hypoglycemia after fruit juice is added to her diet. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
quiz_met3_b:6.r: Aldolase B deficiency (hereditary fructose intolerance) can lead to severe, life-threatening hypoglycemia (p. 679). Galactokinase defects cause galactosemia, which would show on milk (p. 678), and lactase deficiency gives acids and gas, not hypoglycemia (p. 676).

1. Fates of glucose (LO 1)
